title: Incision and drainage of an abscess

guidelineVersions: IDSA skin and soft tissue infection guideline (2014)

related.id: MB-143 Excision of a skin lesion
related.why: The same local anaesthetic, checks and sharps

brief.setting: Surgical assessment unit, on a skin model
brief.scenario: Mr Liam Foster, 28, has a 4-day painful swelling on his upper outer right buttock, well away from the anus. It is a 3 cm fluctuant abscess with a narrow rim of redness. He is well, with normal observations, and has agreed to drainage under local anaesthetic. Instruments, local anaesthetic, swabs and dressings are provided.
brief.task: Drain the abscess on the model, talking the examiner through each step, and answer questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Check, anaesthetise, open widely, break loculi, sample, irrigate, dress, safety-net.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: A stab incision that closes over the pus, or missing a necrotising infection.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'll confirm his identity, the site, his consent and any allergies."

grid.label: Checks and consent
grid.fail: Starts without confirming identity, site or consent.
grid.pass: Confirms identity, site and consent (pain, bleeding, recurrence, scar, packing); checks allergies, anticoagulants and diabetes; completes the safety checklist.
grid.high: Confirms it is suitable for local anaesthetic, and says a perianal, deep or very large abscess needs theatre.

grid.label: Necrotising infection red flags (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Doesn't look beyond the abscess, or drains despite spreading necrosis.
grid.pass: Looks for pain out of proportion, hardness or tenderness beyond the redness, crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis and systemic toxicity.
grid.high: Stops and calls the registrar urgently if any are present: a surgical emergency needing theatre, not bedside drainage.

grid.label: Local anaesthetic
grid.fail: Injects into the abscess cavity, or without checking the maximum dose.
grid.pass: Lidocaine with adrenaline; checks allergy and maximum dose; aspirates; infiltrates around and over the abscess.
grid.high: States the 500 mg maximum with adrenaline, and warns that anaesthesia is less complete in inflamed tissue.

grid.label: Incision and drainage
grid.fail: Makes a small stab and squeezes.
grid.borderline: Drains the pus but doesn't break loculi or send a sample.
grid.pass: Incises over the point of maximal fluctuance along skin lines; sends pus for culture; breaks down loculi.
grid.high: Uses a cruciate or elliptical incision to deroof so it can't close early; explores gently with a finger or artery forceps.

grid.label: Irrigation and dressing
grid.fail: Packs tightly without explaining why, or leaves no dressing.
grid.pass: Irrigates with saline; covers with an absorbent dressing; uses a loose wick only if needed for bleeding.
grid.high: Knows the evidence for packing is weak; in perianal abscess, PPAC2 found non-packing less painful without significantly more fistula or recurrence.

grid.label: Sharps (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Leaves the blade or needle on the field.
grid.pass: Disposes of sharps at the point of use into a sharps bin.
grid.high: Never resheathes, and states what to do after a needlestick: bleed, wash, report, occupational health.

grid.label: Antibiotics and aftercare
grid.fail: Gives antibiotics routinely, or none when he has SIRS features.
grid.pass: Antibiotics only for SIRS features or markedly impaired immunity; wound care; safety-nets for spreading redness, fever and recurrence.
grid.high: Uses IDSA's SIRS thresholds: temperature above 38 or below 36°C, pulse above 90, RR above 24, abnormal white count; checks glucose if recurrent.

pass.text: He doesn't need antibiotics: no systemic features and his immunity is normal. Dressing changes, and come back if the redness spreads, he gets a fever, or it recurs.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll confirm his identity, the site and consent: pain, bleeding, recurrence, a scar. Allergies, anticoagulants, diabetes, and a capillary glucose. It's superficial and away from the anus, so local anaesthetic is reasonable; a perianal one would go to theatre.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Examines widely.] Before I start: no pain out of proportion, no hardness beyond the redness, no crepitus, bullae or necrosis, and his observations are normal. If any were present I'd stop and call my registrar.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Lidocaine with adrenaline, 500 mg maximum; he needs far less. [Aspirates, infiltrates around and over the roof.] It won't be as effective in inflamed tissue, so I'll warn him.

failures.move: Draining at the bedside without looking for crepitus, necrosis or systemic toxicity.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: a necrotising infection is missed and definitive debridement is delayed.

failures.move: Leaving sharps on the field or resheathing a needle.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: needlestick risk to the operator and the team.

failures.move: A small stab incision without breaking loculi.
failures.consequence: The skin closes over residual pus and the abscess recurs.

recovery.when: You're asked the local anaesthetic dose
recovery.line: I'd check the product information: with adrenaline the maximum single dose is 500 mg, and I'd use the smallest dose that works.
The evidence is weak; I'd follow local practice and avoid tight packing.

knowledge.fact: Incision and drainage is the treatment for an abscess; send pus for culture.

Antibiotics as an adjunct to drainage only with SIRS features by IDSA's thresholds (temperature above 38 or below 36°C, pulse above 90, RR above 24, abnormal white count) or markedly impaired host defences. Standard SIRS uses RR above 20.
Necrotising infection: pain out of proportion, hardness beyond erythema, crepitus, bullae, necrosis, toxicity. Urgent surgical review.
Perianal abscess (PPAC2): not packing was less painful, with no significant difference in fistula or recurrence.

recall.think: Is this simply an abscess, or a necrotising infection?
recall.say: "No crepitus, bullae or necrosis, and he's systemically well."

numbers.meaning: IDSA's SIRS thresholds (temperature, pulse, RR): consider antibiotics

recall.trap: A stab incision that closes over the pus.
recall.finish: Drained, cultured, dressed, safety-netted; theatre for perianal or deep abscesses.

sources.name: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
sources.supports: Sign in, time out, sign out: identity, site, procedure, consent, allergies; counts at the end

sources.name: IDSA: Practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections (Stevens DL et al., Clin Infect Dis 2014;59:e10-52)
sources.supports: Incision and drainage for abscesses (rec 5); Gram stain and culture of pus recommended (rec 3); antibiotics as an adjunct based on SIRS: temperature above 38 or below 36°C, RR above 24, HR above 90, WCC above 12,000 or below 4,000/µL (printed as <400 in the guideline) (rec 6); antibiotic active against MRSA if initial antibiotics have failed, host defences are markedly impaired, or SIRS with hypotension; prompt surgical consultation for suspected necrotising infection (rec 27); features of deeper infection: pain disproportionate to findings, wooden-hard subcutaneous tissue beyond the skin changes, systemic toxicity, oedema or tenderness beyond erythema, crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis or ecchymoses

sources.name: Newton K, Dumville J, Briggs M, et al. Postoperative Packing of Perianal Abscess Cavities (PPAC2): randomized clinical trial. Br J Surg 2022;109(10):951-957
sources.supports: 433 adults admitted to 50 NHS hospitals for incision and drainage of a primary perianal abscess: non-packing less painful (mean maximum pain 28.2 vs 38.2 of 100); fistula 11% vs 15% and recurrence 6% vs 3%, neither significant

sources.name: Lidocaine 1% with adrenaline 1:200,000 solution for injection: Summary of Product Characteristics (emc 2397)
sources.supports: Maximum single dose of lidocaine given with adrenaline: 500 mg

sources.name: Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 (SI 2013/645)
sources.supports: Employers must minimise sharps risk: safe systems of work, safe disposal, and a response to sharps injuries

partner.opening: Please drain this abscess on the model, talking me through what you are doing.

reveals.finding: Identity and consent confirmed, no allergies, not anticoagulated, no diabetes known, capillary glucose 5.6, 75 kg.

reveals.trigger: Asks about the surrounding skin and observations
reveals.finding: 1 cm rim of redness, no crepitus, bullae or necrosis. Temperature 37.2°C, pulse 82, RR 14.
Say: "There's a lot of pus, and it feels like there are separate pockets."
Watch where the blade and needle go.

push.question: Why a cruciate or elliptical incision rather than a stab?
push.expect: It deroofs the abscess so the skin can't close over residual pus.

push.question: Would you pack it?
push.expect: Not routinely; evidence is weak; PPAC2 in perianal abscess found non-packing less painful.

push.question: When would he need antibiotics?
push.expect: SIRS features, markedly impaired immunity, or failure of initial antibiotics.

curveballs.prompt: The skin around it is dusky with blisters, and he's in severe pain.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Possible necrotising infection: stop, call the registrar, resuscitate, and arrange urgent theatre.

curveballs.prompt: The abscess is next to the anus instead.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Perianal abscess: drainage in theatre under general anaesthetic.

curveballs.prompt: It's his third abscess this year.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider PVL-producing Staphylococcus aureus: send pus for culture requesting PVL testing, ask about household contacts with boils, check for diabetes, and discuss with microbiology (decolonisation if PVL-positive).
